question: You want to create a new Git repository that shares a .git directory with an existing repository, so both repositories have the same commit history and object database. Which approach achieves this without duplicating data?
options: Use git clone --bare followed by git new-worktree-dir, or configure gitdir to point to a shared .git directory
Copy the .git folder from one repository to another
Create two separate repositories and use git remote add to link them
Use git submodule to embed one repository inside another
explanation: git worktree or configuring core.worktreeConfig allows multiple working directories to share a single .git; git new-worktree-dir sets up the linkage without duplication.

question: You initialize a repository with git init, but you want to immediately configure it so that the default branch is main instead of master. Which approach works at initialization time?
options: Use git init -b main or git config --initial-branch main to set the default branch name
Rename master to main with git branch -m master main after initialization
Edit the HEAD file in .git to point to refs/heads/main
Use git symbolic-ref to update HEAD before the first commit
explanation: git init -b main (Git 2.28+) or git config --initial-branch main sets the default branch at initialization; renaming after creation requires special handling for the first commit.

question: You have a monorepo with five independent projects, each with its own package.json and build system. You want to organize them so that each project can have separate CI/CD triggers but share version control history. Which structure should you use?
options: Keep all projects in a single repository with separate directories and use .github/workflows to trigger CI based on path filters
Create five separate repositories and use git submodule to reference them
Use git worktree to create separate checkouts for each project
Create one repository per project and use git merge to combine histories quarterly
explanation: A monorepo with path-based CI triggers in workflows allows independent builds while sharing commit history; submodules complicate workflow and lose history integration.

question: You clone a repository that has a deeply nested .git directory in a subdirectory (due to a misconfiguration). When you run git status, it operates on the nested .git instead of the parent. How do you fix this without losing any commits?
options: Move the nested .git to the repository root and update core.gitdir if needed, or use git rev-parse --git-dir to identify the current git directory
Delete the nested .git and run git init in the root
Clone the repository again to get the correct structure
Run git fsck to repair the corrupted repository structure
explanation: git rev-parse --git-dir shows which .git directory Git is using; moving it to the correct location or updating gitdir in .git/config restores proper operation.

question: You initialize a bare repository (with git init --bare) to use as a central server repository. A developer pushes to it, but the working files are not visible on the server. Is this the expected behavior, and if so, why?
options: Yes, bare repositories store only Git objects and refs without a working directory; they are designed as central repositories, not for development work
No, bare repositories should include working files; you should run git checkout to restore them
No, the developer must have used the wrong branch; switch to main to see files
Yes, but you should create a post-receive hook to run git checkout in a separate worktree
explanation: Bare repositories (created with --bare or .git/config core.bare=true) store objects and refs but no working directory; this prevents merge conflicts when multiple developers push.

question: You want to create a new repository that is based on an existing repository but with its entire history rewritten to exclude sensitive files. What is the correct sequence of operations?
options: Use git clone, then git filter-branch or git filter-repo to rewrite history, then push to the new repository origin
Use git init and manually commit all files from the original repository
Use git subtree to extract the files you want to keep
Clone the repository and use git rebase to rewrite commits selectively
explanation: filter-branch or filter-repo rewrites commit history across all branches; after filtering, force-push to a fresh repository to replace the origin.

question: You create a new repository with git init, then initialize it with an empty initial commit. Why might this be useful?
options: An empty initial commit provides a stable root commit for rebasing, cherry-picking, and history analysis without breaking when reaching the beginning
It improves performance for large repositories
It prevents accidental force-pushes to main
It enables faster cloning by reducing object count
explanation: An empty root commit acts as an anchor; rebasing on top of an implicit root can fail, but an explicit empty commit ensures git log and rebase work predictably.

question: After running git init in a directory, the .gitignore file is not recognized by Git. What is the most likely reason?
options: .gitignore must be committed to the repository for Git to parse it; untracked .gitignore files are ignored by design
The file must be named .git-ignore instead of .gitignore
.gitignore only works after the first commit is made
The core.excludesfile configuration must be set to enable .gitignore
explanation: .gitignore works only when committed because Git reads it from the index; untracked .gitignore files in the working directory are themselves ignored to prevent configuration leaks.

question: You clone a repository and notice the .git folder is suspiciously small (a few KB). When you run git log, it shows only a few commits despite the remote having thousands. What configuration is in place?
options: The repository is a shallow clone (created with --depth or --single-branch); convert it to a full clone with git fetch --unshallow
The repository uses LFS and most files are not downloaded
Git is configured to show only recent commits
The clone operation was corrupted and you need to re-clone
explanation: Shallow clones (--depth N) download only recent history to save bandwidth; git fetch --unshallow converts the repository to a full clone by fetching all missing commits.

question: You initialize a repository with git init but want to immediately add a standard template of files (LICENSE, README, .gitignore) without manual creation. Which Git feature or workflow should you use?
options: Use git init --template to specify a template directory with pre-populated files, or use git init then copy files from a template repository
Use git clone with a template URL
Create a hook that generates files automatically
Use git config to enable a file generation script
explanation: git init --template=<dir> copies files from a template directory into the new repository; templates are useful for enforcing organization standards.
